reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it directs viewers from an advertised flash-loan arbitrage tool to connect MetaMask, pay stated BNB deployment, swapping and gas charges, and click Deposit and Execute before receiving a displayed 4.7437 BNB estimated profit on a 72 BNB loan. The upfront payment-and-deposit requirement is presented as the gateway to a rapid, large return, while the final wallet screen is used to imply success without documenting an actual flash-loan trade or the provenance of the payout.

Today I'll show you how to create flash loan arbitrage using this tools.
The contract deployment fee is 0.05 BNB. Swapping fee is 0.36 BNB. Gas fee is 0.41 BNB and the loan estimated profit or ROI is 4.7437 BNB.

After choosing the loan amount, click connect to Metamask, then wait until notification.

opening.argument: The material includes an explicit operational warning rather than presenting the method as universally safe or guaranteed: “This method does not work on test networks!” It further warns that sending tokens on a testnet causes them to lose value. Those cautions identify technical and financial risk, while the return is described as an estimate, not a promise. A careful viewer is told to distinguish the real network from a test environment and is warned about a specific way funds can become worthless. That context is inconsistent with an undisclosed or risk-free solicitation.

citations.quote: Important Note: This method does not work on test networks!
If you send the tokens on the testnet, your tokens will lose all value.
the loan estimated profit or ROI is 4.7437 BNB

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account emphasizes the displayed fees and wallet connection, but those details do not establish that the creator concealed risk. The description expressly warns about test networks and loss of value, and the narration calls the return an estimated ROI. The instructions therefore present a risky technical process with an explicit limitation, not an unconditional promise of profit.

citations.quote: This method does not work on test networks!
your tokens will lose all value
loan estimated profit or ROI

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A warning about test networks does not warn viewers that the promoted workflow itself may take their funds without producing the stated return. Calling a number an “estimated” ROI still foregrounds a concrete gain, while the video directs the viewer to enter an address, connect a wallet, deposit, and execute. The warning narrows one technical condition; it does not negate the solicitation of an advance transaction.

opening.argument: The presentation is structured as a hands-on technology tutorial. Its title calls itself “Step for Step Guidance,” and the narrator says, “Today I'll show you how to create flash loan arbitrage using this tools.” The sequence explains selecting a token, entering an address, choosing a loan amount, connecting MetaMask, and checking the result. That is recognizable operational instruction about a DeFi workflow, rather than commentary that merely asserts an investment outcome. The interface itself is shown as the object of the demonstration, so the content can be understood as teaching viewers how the tool operates.

citations.quote: Step for Step Guidance
Today I'll show you how to create flash loan arbitrage using this tools.
First thing to do is select crypto token.
after connecting to Metamask, you can start deploying the flash loan contract

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account interprets instructional steps as a solicitation, but the narration repeatedly describes what the viewer should do in a software workflow. It explains token selection, amount selection, wallet connection, deployment, and execution; that procedural structure is consistent with a demonstration of a tool. A displayed estimate inside a tutorial does not by itself prove that the video certifies the outcome.

citations.quote: Step for Step Guidance
the next step is choose a loan amount
Now after connecting to Metamask, you can start deploying the flash loan contract.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling the content a tutorial does not remove its practical solicitation. The instructions do not stop at explaining concepts: they tell viewers to enter their BNB address, connect MetaMask, deposit, confirm, execute, and then check whether the loan was successful. The final claim of success is not an independently documented trade or payout; it is the outcome the workflow encourages viewers to expect.

opening.argument: At most, the material promotes access to an external arbitrage tool or service. The description provides a tool link, and the narration itemizes operational charges: contract deployment, swapping, and gas. Those are presented as transaction-related costs, not as membership fees, recruitment payments, or a request for credentials. The material does not ask for a password or private key, and the displayed workflow concerns a wallet address and transaction confirmations. The return is labeled “estimated profit or ROI,” which leaves room for uncertainty rather than stating that every user will receive a fixed payout.

The contract deployment fee is 0.05 BNB. Swapping fee is 0.36 BNB. Gas fee is 0.41 BNB

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing account treats ordinary transaction steps as proof of a scam mechanism. But the supplied material identifies a tool link and names specific deployment, swapping, and gas charges. It does not show a request for passwords or private keys, recruitment, or a guaranteed fixed return. The existence of costs and wallet interaction is not enough to establish that the service is fraudulent.

The contract deployment fee is 0.05 BNB.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The service framing does not resolve the central mechanism: the viewer is told to connect a wallet, confirm a deposit, and execute after paying listed charges, in exchange for an estimated profit. A private-key request is unnecessary for a harmful transaction flow, and the absence of recruitment does not make the promised arbitrage return reliable. The supplied evidence also does not independently establish that an actual arbitrage trade produced the displayed balance.
